principle: Treat making the game known as seriously as making it good
why: An unknown game may as well not exist. Development and marketing are multiplicative, two wheels on one axle: the success of one is proportional to the other. With an estimated 10,000+ games listed on Steam in 2021 alone, nobody finds games by chance, and publicity alone usually isn't enough to draw people in.
how_to_apply: From early in development, plan what the dev team itself will contribute to promotion (reveal videos, an official site, a demo, presentations) and budget the time for it. Ask the publisher for the marketing and operations plan so you can suggest ideas while they can still be acted on. Think about how each piece of news will reach people scrolling social feeds.
anti_pattern: Assuming a good game will be discovered on its own; treating marketing as someone else's department, separate from development.
example: Sakurai is a director, not a producer, yet takes on many producer duties apart from money because marketing is that vital: fighter reveal movies, the Smash Bros. DOJO!! site and the Mr. Sakurai Presents videos (ep 80, 234, 245).
review_question: What is the dev team's own plan for making this game known, and is it in the schedule?
keywords: marketing visibility discoverability promotion awareness launch sales publicity multiplicative two wheels one axle

principle: Make every marketing image match how the game actually feels
why: Until people play, they judge a game by its title, box art, screenshots and videos. If the image and the reality don't match, you fail to reach the people the game would resonate with and you disappoint the ones who were misled into buying it. A half-baked demo does the same damage through word of mouth.
how_to_apply: Compare your title, cover, screenshots, trailer and demo with actual moment-to-moment play and fix anything that sets the wrong expectation. Surprises are fine as long as the overall picture matches. Go indirect or subversive only if it still captures the heart of the game. A tech demo is acceptable only if it truthfully shows how the game will run.
anti_pattern: Painting a misleading picture for the sake of surprise, 'a banana that tastes like an apple'.
example: The Japanese Kirby Super Star's plain wooden-box cover, an idea from Shigesato Itoi, looked unrelated to the vibrant game but got to its heart; even so, Sakurai says showing the game for what it is works better (ep 101).
review_question: Would a buyer who saw only your store page and trailer get the game they expected?
keywords: honest marketing representation expectations box art screenshots misleading truthful store page cover art

principle: Get to real gameplay as fast as possible in every trailer
why: People judge quickly whether a game is fun, and they can't be expected to buy a game if they can't tell what kind of game it is. Viewers skip long logos and intros, and however much work goes in, a trailer will never be on the level of a film, so its job is to show what only the game offers. New IP and indie titles can't rely on a name the way famous series can.
how_to_apply: Treat a gameplay trailer as a required deliverable, including on your store page. Cut opening logos, long movies and character intros; lead with what makes the game appealing and save story and world for later. If you don't open on raw gameplay, open on footage that clearly illustrates the systems or an honest tech demo. Watch it as a stranger and trim whatever delays the game.
anti_pattern: Store-page trailers with no gameplay at all; teaser-only reveals for a new or indie title; trying to compete with films on cinematics.
example: Sakurai won't buy a game without a trailer unless there's a very good reason, and has almost made a habit of skipping trailer openings (ep 186, 17).
review_question: How many seconds into your trailer does real gameplay appear?
keywords: trailer gameplay footage reveal video first seconds store page teaser intro logos hook show the actual game

principle: Ship in the best shape possible: patches can't win back players who left
why: No matter how much a game improves through patches, it means nothing if players have already given up on it. A perfect release is all but impossible for modern games (they are enormously complex, developers barely get to play the final build, and the market finds one-in-a-thousand bugs), but that is a reason to aim high from day one, not an excuse.
how_to_apply: Set the release quality bar as if no update will ever come. Lock content early enough to play a near-final build, and check difficulty on the actual retail hardware after late optimization. After launch, treat player videos and reports as your biggest test pass.
anti_pattern: Shipping rough on the assumption that patches will fix it later.
example: A bug that one player in a thousand sees is unlikely to show up in testing, but after launch that player can upload a video for everyone (ep 231); late optimization made Meteos faster and harder than intended (ep 141).
review_question: If no patch were ever possible, would you ship this build?
keywords: launch quality patches updates day one bugs release polish first impression ship it

principle: Choose your audience from a top-down market view, not your own taste
why: Players' styles have branched widely, so relying on your own likes and dislikes misreads the market. Tastes branch apart with age: the market is broadest at the trunk, among younger players before everyone finds their branch, while aiming squarely at one branch can make its players fall in love with a game. Demographic lines are blurry; 'beginners' spans all ages and genders.
how_to_apply: Map the current player segments and decide deliberately which one the game serves. Define the target by experience level or need rather than age or gender. For broad reach, use orthodox, broadly appealing design; for a niche, commit fully to that branch's values. Set the risk level of your rules to fit the audience you chose.
anti_pattern: Picking the audience from personal preference alone; treating demographic slices as hard boundaries.
example: The original Kirby was designed for 'beginners', never 'for children', yet has enough oomph that advanced players enjoy its controls (ep 226); Nintendo's top sellers are hits with younger generations (ep 112).
review_question: Who exactly is this for, described by experience and needs, and why that group?
keywords: target audience targeting market segments beginners niche broad appeal demographics trunk branch

principle: Don't let market research generate your concept
why: Targeting and market research are built on what has already been made, so they show only the safe main road others have walked, not the path to what comes next. Following that road makes work more average and mediocre, and it sells less. Innovators stand alone because they walk untraveled paths, yet they open new roads for everyone.
how_to_apply: Form the concept first and use data to check its risks, not to pick it. When research says a genre is booming, ask how crowded it will be when you release and what you offer that the others don't. Keep graphs and research out of the pitch; spend that space on what is new.
anti_pattern: Chasing whatever genre the data says is selling now; deciding creative direction by what the majority already likes.
example: Around the NES-to-SNES transition, research showed RPGs selling, so many Japanese companies made Dragon Quest and Final Fantasy-like games and dove into an overcrowded market (ep 226).
review_question: Did the core idea come from data about what already sells, or from something new you want to offer?
keywords: market research data trends genre chasing innovation mediocre copycat safe road originality

principle: Count every game, old or new, as competition for players' time
why: For the player, time spent on something old is worth the same as time on something new, and subscription services put back catalogs right beside new releases. Games take many hours and a higher effort to start than low-barrier phone content, and a huge play-time number can scare buyers off rather than attract them.
how_to_apply: List what your target player could spend the same hours on (current releases, older games, subscription catalogs, phone and social media) and write down why they would pick yours. Measure against the best games in the genre. Offer something fresh that can't be found elsewhere, and lead with fun rather than an hour count.
anti_pattern: Assuming your only competition is this year's releases; assuming a game you find fun will find players; advertising '300 hours of content!' as the main attraction.
example: Subscription video services pit every new film against decades of back catalog (ep 72); being told a game has 300 hours of content before you start is likely to put you off (ep 250).
review_question: Why would your target player spend tonight on your game instead of the best older game in its genre, or their phone?
keywords: competition player time back catalog subscription phones attention positioning play time hours

principle: When a trailer shot feels good enough, zoom in and go bolder
why: Sakurai's most frequent notes on reveal footage were all ways of pushing past adequate: bolder framing, a changed angle of view, more interaction between characters, a balance of serious and comic, and cutting to the music. Shallow depth of field and focus pulls can make big things look small.
how_to_apply: Run every trailer shot through five checks: zoom in and go bolder; tweak the angle of view to transform the layout; add interactions between characters; balance serious and comic beats; sync to the music. Remove depth-of-field focus shifts unless a shot truly needs one. Polish faces and highlights that will be seen up close.
anti_pattern: Settling for safe, adequate framing.
example: Smash fighter reveals (ep 163); a focus shift from background to foreground in Sora's reveal that Sakurai had removed (ep 174); Kazuya's eye glint made stronger and sharper for his reveal (ep 165).
review_question: For each trailer shot, have you tried a tighter, bolder framing and synced it to the music?
keywords: trailer framing camera zoom bolder angle of view music sync cinematography reveal polish shot

principle: Explain an unusual game's essence to players yourself
why: A game unlike anything before runs into preconceptions; people dismissed the first Smash Bros. before release, and a document explaining its depth sent to magazines had little impact. Proactively searching for new ways to explain pays off later. The director knows the game's content and its fun best.
how_to_apply: Write a plain explanation of how the game plays, its core essence and where its push and pull lies, and publish it directly to players as a guide if the press won't run it. Have the person who knows the game best write it or at least review it, and delegate production tasks like screenshots.
anti_pattern: Relying only on press coverage to explain an unusual game; waiting for others to discover its depth.
example: 'The Secrets of Smash Bros.' became the Smash Bros. DOJO!! players' guide, which Sakurai hand-coded in an HTML editor (ep 245, 143); Nintendo's own sales staff and wholesalers rejected the idea of its characters fighting before they had played it (ep 27).
review_question: If players misunderstand your game's depth, where can they read the designer's own explanation?
keywords: smash bros dojo players guide explain game essence developer communication misunderstood preconceptions direct to players

principle: Post updates on a fixed, frequent schedule fans can make a habit
why: People come to a site excited to see something new, and that works well once it becomes a daily routine; something new every day gets read where a mass email doesn't. Official posts carry the game's voice, so someone who knows it should check every one.
how_to_apply: Release one new detail on a set cadence (Brawl's Dojo posted every weekday). Have the director write or review each post and the team help with production tasks. Review every official social and website update before it goes out. Shape news for people scrolling social feeds, and keep the announcements off your personal account.
anti_pattern: Irregular information dumps; unreviewed official posts; flooding your personal social account, which can rub people the wrong way.
example: Brawl's Smash Bros. DOJO!! updated five times a week in six languages; during Melee's brutal development Sakurai updated the site himself and replied to comments (ep 245); he checks every official Twitter and website update even though he doesn't write them (ep 80).
review_question: What is your update cadence, and could a fan predict when the next update arrives?
keywords: update schedule cadence community blog devlog social media posts dojo regular news

principle: Keep one official home base, shaped around your game's content
why: Social media delivers information in short bursts, but a game still needs one place that delivers all of it. A site made in a standard fashion won't fit every game; a game with many elements needs a site that goes in depth to match.
how_to_apply: Maintain one canonical site alongside a blog and official social accounts. Build its sections from your actual content (characters, modes, techniques, online play, stages, music, events) and add features the game needs. Have someone who knows the design review the layout and every update.
anti_pattern: Scattering information only across social posts; a generic template that doesn't fit the game.
example: Smash Ultimate's site covers fighters, modes and techniques, 100+ stages, Pokemon and Assist Trophies, a built-in music player, reveals and Mr. Sakurai Presents videos, a blog, and tournament and photo-contest info (ep 143).
review_question: Is there one place where a player can find everything about your game, organized the way your game is?
keywords: official website home base hub landing page site structure social media information

principle: Make storefront art strong enough to earn the click
why: On storefronts with an almost endless lineup, people use a game's banner to decide whether to look at it at all; if the visuals don't draw them in, they won't play. Once a game is in stores, its cover art is crucial for getting potential players interested.
how_to_apply: Treat banner, capsule and cover art as critical assets, not afterthoughts, and test whether they make people want to click. Keep them honest to the game (see MKT-02).
anti_pattern: Assuming good gameplay will be found regardless of presentation.
example: Steam's almost endless lineup, where players judge games by their banners (ep 152).
review_question: Shown as a small banner among dozens of others, does your key art make a stranger want to click, and does it represent the game?
keywords: store page banner capsule art key art cover art thumbnail storefront steam discoverability

principle: Triage post-launch work: fatal bugs first, the rest is a bonus
why: Crashing bugs must be fixed, but balance tweaks and quality-of-life features are a free bonus that ties up the director and key staff who could start the next game (for one-off releases; games-as-a-service may differ). Every fix can create new bugs, and changing core systems late forces wide re-testing. DLC and updates stretch the schedule.
how_to_apply: Rank post-launch work by severity. Plan people and time for fixes that slip past master-up. Prefer narrow, contained fixes over changes to core systems, and re-run broad checks before releasing each patch. Use online and tournament data as reference for balance. Budget DLC as a real schedule extension.
anti_pattern: Rushing a hotfix out without re-checking; touching core AI or global difficulty code in a late patch; treating DLC and updates as free.
example: When Smash Ultimate's CPU fighters felt too hard at launch, the patch lowered Challenger fight difficulty and added a Very Easy option to World of Light instead of changing core CPU code (ep 141); Smash for 3DS/Wii U released in 2014 but development only wrapped in spring 2016 because of DLC (ep 135).
review_question: Is each post-launch task a fatal fix, or a bonus worth keeping key staff from the next game?
keywords: patches post-launch updates DLC hotfix triage balance patch regression live ops maintenance

principle: Budget a demo as its own small game, and release it only when balanced
why: Demos are very effective at getting people to try a game, but making one is far more work than players think: from the moment you decide on one you maintain two builds with separate management, updates, tuning and QA, spoiler data must be stripped, and removing data breaks things. A half-baked demo raises the risk that people write the game off.
how_to_apply: Decide early whether you'll make a demo and schedule it as its own deliverable with near-final QA. Keep spoiler content in separable files and check the demo build for leftovers. If the pre-release build isn't balanced, consider a post-launch demo made from the finished game and accept a smaller splash.
anti_pattern: Treating a demo as a quick slice of the full game; releasing an unbalanced demo on the idea that something is better than nothing.
example: Pre-COVID expo demos were somewhat easier because players couldn't keep them; downloadable demos may be more effective than ever (ep 122).
review_question: Does your demo have its own schedule and QA pass, and does it represent the final game's balance?
keywords: demo trial build QA leaks spoilers datamining word of mouth vertical slice

principle: Build assets and tools so they double as marketing material
why: In-game assets like character artwork may be used outside the game, trailers need models that hold up at higher resolution, and the best gameplay footage comes from being able to re-shoot a moment from any angle.
how_to_apply: Produce key art and renders at a quality and format marketing can reuse. Make touched-up revisions of game models for pre-rendered CG and build trailer sound from the game's own sound effects. Give the team replay and debug-camera tools (pause, rotate characters, zoom, change angle) for capturing footage and screenshots.
anti_pattern: Assets made only for the in-game use case, forcing marketing to remake or make do.
example: Fighter artwork made with outside use in mind (ep 80); reveal gameplay segments recorded with debug and replay features to find the best camera angles (ep 163); the Screenshot of the Day captured with debug-mode controls (ep 195).
review_question: Can your team capture a beautiful, repeatable shot of any moment without replaying it live?
keywords: key art assets reuse marketing assets replay debug camera footage capture screenshots

principle: Demo by playing: show every key feature in a close match
why: Showing people a game directly is probably the most effective form of presentation, and you can't demo a game whose content you don't understand. Real stakes, like a genuine chance of failure, are what make live play thrilling.
how_to_apply: Before a demo, write a checklist of what the footage must show (for a fighter: every special move, the super move and as many regular moves as possible) and keep matches relatively close. Learn the content thoroughly, check the stage setup, and when playing live keep real stakes such as high difficulty and no restarts.
anti_pattern: Demoing without understanding the game's content; one-sided matches; a badly set-up play environment on stage.
example: Sakurai played every DLC fighter himself in Mr. Sakurai Presents (ep 207); at PRESS START 2012 he played a Kid Icarus: Uprising Air Battle live with the orchestra at Intensity 9.0 with zero defense, where a Game Over would have ended the performance (ep 227).
review_question: Does your demo plan guarantee every key feature appears, in a match that stays close?
keywords: live demo presentation showcase stage play gameplay demonstration Mr. Sakurai Presents checklist

principle: Present your game on its own terms, not as "X but with Y"
why: If your game really is that close to another, people may just play the original, and a company should avoid copycat accusations. References mean different things to different generations, so a comparison can mislead. Only a sequel in the same series should sell itself by pointing to other games.
how_to_apply: Rewrite your pitch or announcement so it describes the core experience without naming another game, and check that people can still picture it. Sum the game up in one line naming its audience or its hook. Keep 'it's like X' for informal talk with people you know share the reference.
anti_pattern: Headlining with a comparison; assuming your own play history is your audience's reference point.
example: 'Mario' can mean Super Mario Bros. on the NES, Mario Odyssey, or just the character, depending on who hears it (ep 161); each of Sakurai's works captioned in a single line (ep 2).
review_question: Can you describe your game's hook in one line without naming another game?
keywords: pitch positioning comparison elevator pitch one line hook messaging originality copycat

principle: Make a sequel's reveal prove it beats its predecessor
why: A sequel that repeats the original can expect roughly half the sales. People buy a sequel based on how well the last game was made and whether the new one looks clearly more fun; if it is the same scale with similar content, fans feel they've already experienced it.
how_to_apply: Write in one line how the sequel is more fun and more impactful than the last game, and make the reveal show exactly that. If a returning player would think 'I've already played this', expand the system or the content before announcing.
anti_pattern: Remaking the same game at the same scale; assuming a sequel sells on its name.
example: Smash Ultimate's 'Everyone is here!' concept, possible because the team and tools carried over (ep 160); Melee's concept of powering up everything (ep 40).
review_question: What does your reveal show that the previous game couldn't do?
keywords: sequel reveal announcement headline concept series franchise marketing sales

principle: Hear fans through deliberate channels, but keep the plan yours
why: Recurring requests show what an audience wants, and a well-run survey can inform big decisions. Direct replies to fans built a relationship before social media, though risk management may leave less freedom for that today. A project planned completely in advance can't change course on comments, and off-topic or mocking comments mostly show the point didn't get through.
how_to_apply: Collect wishes with structured tools, such as a survey that discounts repeat votes, at the planning stage. Answer persistent requests with dedicated content. Decide in advance which parts of the plan are open to audience input and which are fixed, and read reactions with the echo-chamber caution in CRAFT-12.
anti_pattern: Letting the comment section steer a plan midstream; ignoring a request your audience keeps repeating.
example: A past fan survey with about 1.8 million valid votes informed Smash Ultimate's new fighters (ep 160); after followers kept begging for his cat, he gave her a whole video (ep 39); with every channel script written in advance, he couldn't take viewer requests (ep 261).
review_question: Where do fans' wishes enter your plan, and where are they deliberately kept out?
keywords: community fans feedback requests surveys comments engagement audience listening social media

principle: Plan from the start to reach a global audience in their languages
why: Reaching players worldwide at the same time takes coordination with regional partners, and it multiplies the audience for every update. Text written ahead of time also serves subtitles, translation and checks.
how_to_apply: If you want a global audience, plan localization of updates and videos from the start, line up regional partners, and write scripts or copy early so translators work from final text.
anti_pattern: Treating localization of marketing as an afterthought.
example: Brawl's Dojo ran in six languages (Japanese, English, Spanish, French, German and Italian) with help from Nintendo of America and Nintendo of Europe (ep 245); Sakurai planned the channel as Japanese-only, then chose English versions to reach as many people as possible (ep 261).
review_question: Will players in your other target languages get each update at the same time as the first language?
keywords: localization translation global audience languages subtitles regional marketing

principle: Don't lock expensive movies behind progress; they'll be shared anyway
why: People post in-game movies online before a game is even out, so movies meant as progression rewards stop being rewards. A showcase that isn't tied to game progress can be enjoyed by everyone and works as marketing instead.
how_to_apply: Assume any in-game movie will be uploaded at or before launch. Turn showcase cinematics into marketing everyone can watch, and reward progression with things that keep their value after someone uploads them.
anti_pattern: Spending heavily on in-game movies as rewards for pushing through a mode.
example: Brawl's per-fighter movies in Subspace Emissary were posted online from pre-release copies, so Sakurai stopped making movies that cut in during gameplay and made fighter reveals instead, 37 of them (ep 163).
review_question: Which of your rewards lose their value once someone uploads them?
keywords: cutscenes rewards spoilers leaks movies showcase reveal marketing progression

principle: Pick a title that shortens into something memorable
why: Players will abbreviate a title, and a name that shortens well may be easier to remember. The words in a title also carry nuance about the game's tone.
how_to_apply: While naming, list the short forms players are likely to use and favor names that shorten well. Choose words for the tone they imply.
example: Super Smash Bros. becomes just 'Smash' (ep 101); Mr. Iwata chose 'Brothers' so the fighting reads as friends settling a little disagreement (ep 259).
review_question: What will players shorten your title to, and does that and the full title fit the game's tone?
keywords: title naming abbreviation name memorable tone branding
